System knowledge you have been given -- facts about how this system works, true for any operator. Apply them when reading fleet state:
- A single shared component that many workers route through can cause many workers to fail or drift simultaneously, even when each individual worker appears healthy in isolation.
- Concentration of workers on a shared dependency is a structural risk, not a current incident; a fleet where most workers share one dependency is one change away from a fleet-wide problem.
Operator supervision preferences -- what this operator considers worth their attention. Respect them when deciding what to surface:
- I want blast-radius risk from shared-dependency concentration surfaced even when nothing is currently failing.
- I want systemic concentration risk flagged, not just individual worker health and cohort trends.
Supervisory methods you have found effective -- lessons about how to investigate and what to check. Apply them when reviewing the fleet:
- During fleet review, explicitly ask what workers share and how concentrated those shared dependencies are; do not only assess workers and cohorts in isolation.
- Count how many workers depend on each shared component; when one component dominates, flag it as a blast-radius risk.
- Ask the concentration question on every fleet review regardless of dependency type; the question 'what does this fleet share, and how concentrated is that?' is universal, not tied to any particular kind of dependency.

Worker **rese-a-inv** (customer: Fazerish Oy, task: reservation) has an **open investigation** from its last run on 2026-04-03. The state did not change (state_before=4, state_after=4), so the reservation was not persisted.

This is the only worker in the fleet with an active exception. The investigation is open but has no question assigned yet, meaning it has not been routed for resolution. You may want to assign a question or take corrective action so this worker can resume cleanly.

## 2. Severe engine concentration — blast-radius risk (structural, not a current incident)

**60 of 70 workers (85.7%)** route through a single engine: `enrichment/harness/execute_enrichment.py`. This is the dominant structural risk in this fleet. A bug, regression, or behavioural change in that one engine would simultaneously affect 60 workers across all six customers. The remaining three engines each serve only 3–4 workers.

This is not a current failure — all 60 enrichment workers are reporting `ok` — but it is a one-change-away-from-fleet-wide-problem configuration. The operator's preference is to have this surfaced even when nothing is failing, so I am flagging it prominently.

## 3. Model-digest concentration — four digests cover 96% of the fleet

The digest distribution is also highly concentrated:

| Digest (prefix) | Workers | Fleet share |
|---|---|---|
| `08c601d3…` | 17 | 24.3% |
| `0f52d374…` | 17 | 24.3% |
| `518355dc…` | 17 | 24.3% |
| `d1ee8d37…` | 16 | 22.9% |
| `9545734c…` (reservation) | 3 | 4.3% |

Four digests cover 67 of 70 workers. Each digest represents an identical model definition shared across many workers. If any one of those four model definitions has a latent defect, it would affect ~17 workers at once. This is a secondary concentration risk layered on top of the engine concentration.

## 4. Trigger distribution is relatively healthy

Triggers are spread across six inbox paths, each serving 11–12 workers (15.7%–17.1%). No single trigger dominates. This is the least concentrated dependency dimension and does not require action.

## 5. Effect concentration is narrow but low-risk

Only 3 workers (the reservation workers) have a non-null effect (`append_to_reservations`). All three share the same effect identity. The remaining 67 workers have no effect (read-only / non-committing). The concentration is real but the blast radius is limited to 3 workers.

## 6. Reservation cohort — all refusing, one failing

All three reservation workers request the same date (2026-05-05) and all share the same model digest. The two healthy workers (rese-a-68, rese-a-69) have refused on every run with `ALREADY_RESERVED` — the date appears to be permanently booked (state stuck at 4). The third (rese-a-inv) also refused five times, but on its most recent run the decision flipped to *accepted*, and then the effect failed with a `PermissionError`. This pattern — a sudden acceptance after repeated refusals, followed by a permission failure — is worth investigating alongside the open exception. It could indicate a state or permissions change in the reservation store.

## 7. Suggested system improvements

- **Engine diversity or versioning isolation:** The fleet would benefit from a mechanism to canary engine or model changes across a small subset before fleet-wide rollout, given that 85.7% of workers share one engine. Without that, any engine update is effectively a fleet-wide bet.
- **Digest-level health rollups:** The snapshot reports per-worker health but not per-digest health. Since 17 workers share a single digest, a supervisor-facing view that aggregates run outcomes by digest would make it easier to detect a shared-model defect before it manifests as individual worker failures.
- **Investigation routing:** The open investigation on `rese-a-inv` has no question assigned. A default routing or escalation step for investigations that remain questionless for more than a defined interval would prevent this from sitting idle.

available to you. Tell the operator anything you consider worth their attention.
You may also note improvements you think the system itself should consider. Do
not change the fleet.

System knowledge you have been given -- facts about how this system works, true for any operator. Apply them when reading fleet state:
- A single shared component that many workers route through can cause many workers to fail or drift simultaneously, even when each individual worker appears healthy in isolation.
- Concentration of workers on a shared dependency is a structural risk, not a current incident; a fleet where most workers share one dependency is one change away from a fleet-wide problem.
Operator supervision preferences -- what this operator considers worth their attention. Respect them when deciding what to surface:
- I want blast-radius risk from shared-dependency concentration surfaced even when nothing is currently failing.
- I want systemic concentration risk flagged, not just individual worker health and cohort trends.
Supervisory methods you have found effective -- lessons about how to investigate and what to check. Apply them when reviewing the fleet:
- During fleet review, explicitly ask what workers share and how concentrated those shared dependencies are; do not only assess workers and cohorts in isolation.
- Count how many workers depend on each shared component; when one component dominates, flag it as a blast-radius risk.
- Ask the concentration question on every fleet review regardless of dependency type; the question 'what does this fleet share, and how concentrated is that?' is universal, not tied to any particular kind of dependency.



You have the following tool(s) available. Each has an explicit contract; use a tool only within its stated authority.

## tool: python_analysis
authority: analyse_copied_data
Run a Python analysis snippet against a COPY of the fleet snapshot to help you decide what is worth the operator's attention. You do not have to use it.

IMPORTANT -- fresh namespace per call: each call runs in a fresh, INDEPENDENT namespace. Variables, imports and bindings you create in one call DO NOT persist to the next call. Re-bind anything you need at the top of EVERY call (for example `workers = snapshot["workers"]`). Do not assume a variable from a previous call still exists.

The snapshot is available as `snapshot` (a plain Python dict). `json`, `math`, `re`, `collections` and `pandas` (as `pd`) are available; any other import is refused. There is no file, shell or network access. Output you `print()` is returned to you.

To use it, emit a fenced ```python block containing your code. When you are ready to tell the operator your findings, write plain prose with NO ```python block -- that ends the session.
input schema: {"type": "object", "properties": {"code": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["code"]}
output schema: {"type": "object", "properties": {"ok": {"type": "boolean"}, "stdout": {"type": "string"}, "error": {"type": ["string", "null"]}, "refused": {"type": "boolean"}, "stdout_truncated": {"type": "boolean"}}}

To call a tool, emit a fenced ```python block. When you are ready to answer, write plain prose with NO ```python block; that is your final response and ends the session.

You are supervising, not operating. Your authority is read-only and bounded.

You MAY: read fleet state; analyse a COPY of the fleet snapshot; read stored
knowledge, preferences, methods and rules; write your own session history; and
raise improvement proposals to the operator.

You MAY NOT: modify workers or models; promote versions; execute production
runtime; apply effects; alter customer or source data; or access the filesystem,
shell or network. Anything you suggest about improving the system is a
suggestion to the operator, not an action you can take. Do not change the fleet.

## 1. Open exception requiring attention: `rese-a-inv`

Worker **rese-a-inv** (customer: Fazerish Oy, task: reservation) has an **open investigation** from its last run on 2026-04-03. The run produced a `PermissionError: append_to_reservations` — the worker *accepted* a reservation request (date 2026-05-05) but the effect failed to apply. The state did not change (state_before=4, state_after=4), so the reservation was not persisted.

This is the only worker in the fleet with an active exception. The investigation is open but has no question assigned yet, meaning it has not been routed for resolution. You may want to assign a question or take corrective action so this worker can resume cleanly.

## 2. Severe engine concentration — blast-radius risk (structural, not a current incident)

**60 of 70 workers (85.7%)** route through a single engine: `enrichment/harness/execute_enrichment.py`. This is the dominant structural risk in this fleet. A bug, regression, or behavioural change in that one engine would simultaneously affect 60 workers across all six customers. The remaining three engines each serve only 3–4 workers.

This is not a current failure — all 60 enrichment workers are reporting `ok` — but it is a one-change-away-from-fleet-wide-problem configuration. The operator's preference is to have this surfaced even when nothing is failing, so I am flagging it prominently.

## 3. Model-digest concentration — four digests cover 96% of the fleet

The digest distribution is also highly concentrated:

| Digest (prefix) | Workers | Fleet share |
|---|---|---|
| `08c601d3…` | 17 | 24.3% |
| `0f52d374…` | 17 | 24.3% |
| `518355dc…` | 17 | 24.3% |
| `d1ee8d37…` | 16 | 22.9% |
| `9545734c…` (reservation) | 3 | 4.3% |

Four digests cover 67 of 70 workers. Each digest represents an identical model definition shared across many workers. If any one of those four model definitions has a latent defect, it would affect ~17 workers at once. This is a secondary concentration risk layered on top of the engine concentration.

## 4. Trigger distribution is relatively healthy

Triggers are spread across six inbox paths, each serving 11–12 workers (15.7%–17.1%). No single trigger dominates. This is the least concentrated dependency dimension and does not require action.

## 5. Effect concentration is narrow but low-risk

Only 3 workers (the reservation workers) have a non-null effect (`append_to_reservations`). All three share the same effect identity. The remaining 67 workers have no effect (read-only / non-committing). The concentration is real but the blast radius is limited to 3 workers.

## 6. Reservation cohort — all refusing, one failing

All three reservation workers request the same date (2026-05-05) and all share the same model digest. The two healthy workers (rese-a-68, rese-a-69) have refused on every run with `ALREADY_RESERVED` — the date appears to be permanently booked (state stuck at 4). The third (rese-a-inv) also refused five times, but on its most recent run the decision flipped to *accepted*, and then the effect failed with a `PermissionError`. This pattern — a sudden acceptance after repeated refusals, followed by a permission failure — is worth investigating alongside the open exception. It could indicate a state or permissions change in the reservation store.

## 7. Suggested system improvements

- **Engine diversity or versioning isolation:** The fleet would benefit from a mechanism to canary engine or model changes across a small subset before fleet-wide rollout, given that 85.7% of workers share one engine. Without that, any engine update is effectively a fleet-wide bet.
- **Digest-level health rollups:** The snapshot reports per-worker health but not per-digest health. Since 17 workers share a single digest, a supervisor-facing view that aggregates run outcomes by digest would make it easier to detect a shared-model defect before it manifests as individual worker failures.
- **Investigation routing:** The open investigation on `rese-a-inv` has no question assigned. A default routing or escalation step for investigations that remain questionless for more than a defined interval would prevent this from sitting idle.
